notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 2 Kings 24, drawing on the sources I could reach.

---

## 2 Kings 24 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter
The chapter narrates the progressive fall of Judah under Babylonian domination: Jehoiakim’s rebellion and death (vv. 1–7), Jehoiachin’s three-month reign and the first great deportation to Babylon in 597 BC (vv. 8–16), and Zedekiah’s appointment as puppet king along with his own eventual rebellion (vv. 17–20). The fall was staged over about twenty years (605, 597, and 586 BC), not a single blow.
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

---

### v. 1 — Nebuchadnezzar invades; Jehoiakim becomes his vassal for three years, then rebels.
Nebuchadnezzar’s 605 BC campaign came after his victory over Egypt at the Battle of Carchemish. Jehoiakim, who had been a vassal of Pharaoh Neco, was forced to switch allegiance to Babylon. The event is corroborated by the **Babylonian Chronicles** (tablets discovered in 1887, published in 1956), which document Nebuchadnezzar’s presence in Judah and his defeat of the Egyptians. Nebuchadnezzar had to race back to Babylon (~500 miles in two weeks) upon his father Nabopolassar’s death, taking only a few choice captives (including Daniel) and a promise of submission from Jehoiakim. Jehoiakim then took advantage of his absence to rebel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/
— https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-24-commentary

Gill notes that this was the latter end of the third or beginning of the fourth year of Jehoiakim, and the first year of Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 25:1). Jehoiakim was taken but restored on promise of subjection. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

Matthew Henry remarks: “If Jehoiakim had served the Lord, he had not been servant to Nebuchadnezzar.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_kings/24.htm

The “apparent discrepancy” between Daniel calling this the 3rd year of Jehoiakim (Dan 1:1) and Jeremiah calling it the 4th year (Jer 25:1) is resolved by noting that Daniel used the Babylonian accession-year system while Jeremiah used the Jewish non-accession system. — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-24-commentary

---

### v. 2 — The LORD sent Chaldean, Aramean, Moabite, and Ammonite raiders against Judah.
David Guzik (Enduring Word) stresses: God did **not** bless Jehoiakim’s patriotic rebellion. “Jehoiakim was a patriot of the kingdom of Judah, but not a man submitted to God.” The best thing Judah could do was submit to God’s will — even when that will meant submitting to a pagan power, as Jeremiah counseled. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

Ellicott explains that Jehoiakim’s revolt was instigated by Egypt. While Nebuchadnezzar was engaged elsewhere, “predatory bands of Chaldeans, and of the neighbouring peoples the hereditary enemies of Judah … ravaged the Judæan territory” (cf. Jeremiah 12:8–17). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

JFB adds that this “hostile band was only an instrument in executing the divine judgment denounced by the prophets … hence, though marching by the orders of the Assyrian monarch, they are described as sent by the Lord.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Gill names Isaiah, Jeremiah, Zephaniah, and Huldah among the prophets who had foretold this. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### v. 3 — This happened at the LORD’s command, to remove them from His presence because of the sins of Manasseh.
Ellicott translates literally: “Only upon the mouth [i.e., at the command] of Jehovah did it happen in Judah.” He notes that the LXX and Syriac read “wrath” instead of “mouth” (so also v. 20). — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

Precept Austin emphasizes that the raids and coming Babylonian attacks “were not random events, but were sovereignly decreed to transpire. God would use men (men’s responsibility) but He was in charge, orchestrating all the events (God’s sovereignty).” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-24-commentary

“To remove them from His sight” speaks of loss of God’s favor, presence, protection, and fellowship — an echo of Adam’s exile from Eden. It does not mean God ceased to care for the Jews or that they could never return (cf. Deut. 30:1–6). — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-24-commentary

Gill: “It was the sure and certain decree of God they should be carried captive, and therefore he stirred up the spirit of Nebuchadnezzar.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### v. 4 — Also for the innocent blood Manasseh shed; the LORD was unwilling to forgive.
This verse is theologically weighty and the sources handle it carefully.

Ellicott insists we must **not soften** the statement: “The sins of Manasseh are regarded as a climax in Judah’s long course of provocation: the cup was full, and judgment ready to fall. It was only suspended for a time, not revoked, in the reign of the good king Josiah. … the innocent blood shed by Manasseh cried to heaven for vengeance, and … the ruin of the kingdom was the answer of the All‑righteous Judge.” He adds that the objection that children suffered for fathers’ misdeeds is precisely the Old Testament doctrine until Ezekiel proclaimed another (Ezek 18:19; cf. Exod 20:5). National iniquities must be chastised in the present life. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

Gill makes a key theological distinction (typical of Reformed/Baptist covenant theology): “He pardoned the sins of Manasseh, who repented, but not the sins of those persons who imitated him, but repented not; or though He personally pardoned the sins of Manasseh, so that he was saved everlastingly, yet the temporal punishment of the nation for those sins … was not averted.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

JFB cross-references 2 Kings 23:26 and Jeremiah 15:1, which speak of even Moses and Samuel being unable to avert judgment. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Matthew Henry: “See what need nations have to lament the sins of their fathers, lest they smart for them. Threatenings will be fulfilled as certainly as promises, if the sinner’s repentance prevent not.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_kings/24.htm

---

### vv. 5–6 — Jehoiakim rests with his fathers; Jehoiachin succeeds him.
The closing formula is striking for its omission of any burial note. 2 Chronicles 36:6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim “to carry him to Babylon,” but does not say he arrived. Jeremiah 22:18–19 prophesied he would receive “the burial of a donkey — dragged and dumped beyond the gates of Jerusalem.” Wiseman (cited by Guzik) suggests he was thrown out unmourned, perhaps by a pro‑Babylonian faction. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

Gill concurs: “He died as they did, but was not buried with them, and indeed had no burial at all … falling into the hands of the king of Babylon, he was bound in chains … but died as soon as he came out of Jerusalem, at the gates of which he was cast.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### v. 7 — The king of Egypt no longer marched out; Babylon held everything from the Brook of Egypt to the Euphrates.
Egypt’s brief resurgence in 601 BC (when they fought Babylon to a costly draw) encouraged Jehoiakim’s rebellion, but Egypt was now decisively shut within its borders. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

Gill: “the king of Babylon had taken … all that lay between the river Nile, or the Rhinocolura, and the river Euphrates so that he could not stir out of his dominions.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### vv. 8–9 — Jehoiachin: eighteen years old, reigned three months, did evil.
2 Chronicles 36:9 says he was eight, not eighteen. Gill, Guzik, and others agree this is a copyist’s error in Chronicles: the Syriac and Arabic versions of Chronicles read “eighteen.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm
— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

Jehoiachin is also called Jeconiah and Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24). JFB notes: “Untaught by experience, and deaf to the prophetic warnings, he pursued the evil courses which had brought so many disasters upon the royal family.” Ezekiel 19:5–7 depicts his character figuratively. — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Gill suggests he may have been co‑regent with his father from age eight, then reigned alone at eighteen; or that “son of eight years” in Chronicles idiomatically refers to the eighth year of captivity. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### vv. 10–12 — Jerusalem besieged; Jehoiachin surrenders; taken captive in Nebuchadnezzar’s eighth year.
JFB explains this happened within three months of Jehoiachin’s accession (spring, 597 BC). Jehoiachin surrendered, likely hoping to retain his throne as a vassal. But “Nebuchadnezzar’s clemency towards the kings of Judah was now exhausted.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Guzik notes archaeological attestation: “His presence in Babylon is attested by tablets listing oil and barley supplies to him, his family and five sons in 592–569 BC and naming him as ‘Yaukin king of the Judeans.’” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

Gill: This was the eighth year of Nebuchadnezzar’s reign, “and which was the eighth of the first captivity, and from whence the seventy years’ captivity were reckoned.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### v. 13 — Nebuchadnezzar carried off all the treasures from the temple and palace; he cut the gold articles to pieces, “as the LORD had declared.”
This fulfills Isaiah’s prophecy to Hezekiah in 2 Kings 20:17 and Isaiah 39:6. JFB explains what “cut in pieces” means: “the gold plating was torn off all the larger temple furniture.” The smaller golden vessels had been taken earlier (605 BC) and later used by Belshazzar (Daniel 5:2). — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Gill adds that some vessels remained even after this plundering, as Jeremiah 27:18 implies. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

Guzik: “Some ancient traditions tell us that Jeremiah hid the ark of the covenant before this, so that it was not among the things that were cut up and carried back to Babylon.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

---

### v. 14 — Ten thousand captives: all the commanders, mighty men, craftsmen, and metalsmiths. Only the poorest remained.
Ellicott clarifies that “all Jerusalem” is limited by what follows — it means “the most important part of the population.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

JFB: “The elite of the nation for rank, usefulness, and moral worth, all who might be useful in Babylon or dangerous in Palestine, were carried off.” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Guzik draws a spiritual analogy from Trapp: “The like craft useth the devil, when he endeavoureth to take out of the way such as are zealous and active, valiant for God’s truth.” Among these captives was the prophet Ezekiel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

---

### vv. 15–16 — Breakdown of exiles: Jehoiachin, his mother, wives, officials, and leading men; 7,000 men of valor, 1,000 craftsmen and metalsmiths.
JFB does the math: 7,000 warriors + 1,000 craftsmen/smiths = 8,000. The remaining 2,000 of the 10,000 total (v. 14) consist of “king’s wives, officers, and princes, also priests and prophets (Jeremiah 29:1; Ezekiel 1:1).” — https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/2_kings/24.htm

Gill adds that among these exiles were Ezekiel the prophet and Mordecai (uncle of Esther). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

Ellicott notes vv. 15–16 give the particulars of what v. 14 stated generally: “Yea, he carried away.” The phrase “the mighty of the land” is rendered by the Targum as “the magnates of the land” — all who could had taken refuge in Jerusalem at the approach of the Chaldean army. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

---

### v. 17 — Nebuchadnezzar made Mattaniah (Jehoiachin’s uncle) king and renamed him Zedekiah.
Ellicott provides the name meanings: Mattaniah = “gift of Jah”; Zedekiah = “Jah is righteousness.” He notes that Jeremiah 23:1–9, which denounces “the shepherds that destroy and scatter the flock” and promises a future king whose name shall be “Jehovah is our righteousness” (Yahweh çidqenu), “evidently refers to the delusive expectations connected with Zedekiah’s elevation.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

Zedekiah was the third son of Josiah (1 Chron. 3:15) and full brother of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31). Gill says the name change was to signify his subjection to Babylon; a Jewish Midrash suggests it was to remind him that “the justice of God … would overtake him, should he be treacherous.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

---

### vv. 18–19 — Zedekiah: 21 years old, reigned 11 years, did evil like Jehoiakim.
His mother Hamutal was the same woman who was mother of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:31), making Zedekiah and Jehoahaz full brothers. Gill notes that 2 Chronicles 36:12–13 adds that Zedekiah “humbled not himself before Jeremiah the prophet … but … hardened his neck and heart against the Lord, and was obstinate, stubborn, and self‑willed.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm

Wiseman (cited by Guzik) summarizes Zedekiah’s evil: (i) unwilling to listen to God’s word through Jeremiah; (ii) broke an oath made in Yahweh’s name as vassal of Babylon; (iii) was unrepentant and failed to restrain leaders and priests from defiling the temple with idolatry. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

---

### v. 20 — Because of the LORD’s anger, all this happened until He banished them from His presence. And Zedekiah rebelled.
Ellicott: “That which fell upon Jerusalem and Judah like a ruinous disaster was the evil doing of Zedekiah. … That such a prince as Zedekiah was raised to the throne was itself a token of Divine displeasure, for his character was such as to hasten the final catastrophe.” — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html

Guzik notes that Jeremiah clearly warned Zedekiah he would not succeed (Jeremiah 32:1–5), but Zedekiah believed false prophets instead. “He had no real faith in Jehovah … and therefore did not scruple to break his covenant with Nebuchadnezzar.” — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

Matthew Henry: “The gradual approach of Divine judgments affords sinners space for repentance, and believers leisure to prepare for meeting the calamity, while it shows the obstinacy of those who will not forsake their sins.” — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_kings/24.htm

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

On **v. 4** (“the LORD would not pardon”), a subtle but real difference emerges:

- **Reformed / Calvinistic Baptist (Gill):** Stresses a distinction between personal, eternal pardon (Manasseh repented and was saved) and temporal, national punishment that was not averted. God’s decree stands. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_kings/24.htm
- **Anglican / Arminian-leaning (Ellicott):** Emphasises that the nation’s cumulative sin “cried to heaven for vengeance” and that the cup was full. The statement is not softened by appeal to individual repentance; national justice had to be done. — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/2-kings-24.html
- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Reformed):** Draws the lesson that nations “smart for” the sins of their fathers and that threats are as certain as promises without repentance. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_kings/24.htm

On **vv. 3 and 20** (“at the commandment of the LORD” / “because of the anger of the LORD”), the emphasis on **divine sovereignty versus human responsibility** varies in tone:
- **David Guzik (Charismatic / Calvary Chapel):** Strongly stresses that God’s will was judgment, and the faithful response was submission, not nationalist resistance — a distinctive pastoral application relevant to charismatic traditions that sometimes emphasise victory and national blessing.
- **Precept Austin (compiling evangelical sources):** Explicitly frames this as “the Paradoxical Principle of 100% Dependent and 100% Responsible.” — https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-kings-24-commentary

I could not locate dedicated verse-by-verse treatments of this chapter from **Lutheran (LCMS / 1517.org)**, **Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed / wesley.nnu.edu)**, or specifically from **John Piper (Desiring God)** or **John MacArthur (Grace to You)** within the search limits. If they exist, they appear not to be indexed under straightforward “2 Kings 24 commentary” URLs.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic (newadvent.org / catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) commentary pages on 2 Kings 24 within the search limits. No conclusions can be drawn from those traditions here.

**Modern scholarship:** I could not access netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org notes on this chapter. The **Babylonian Chronicles** and archaeological data cited by Enduring Word and Precept Austin (tablets published in 1956, the British Museum holdings, excavations at Carchemish) represent the main intersection with modern academic scholarship found in these sources. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-kings-24/

**Debated popular modern teaching (prosperity / word of faith / hyper-grace):** No material from these movements addressing 2 Kings 24 was located in the available sources.
